title: Reliability intake - fallback & private fit - Quantum Ledger
summary: Discovery focused on whether Redwood Hosted/Dedicated/Private meets Quantum Ledger's low-latency SLA and strict data residency/KMS needs. Discussed multi-region routing, circuit breakers, fallback to smaller models or cache, private deploy fit in their VPC, and proof-of-concept benchmarks. Action items: send security pack, run a latency pilot with synthetic traffic, and align on SLOs for pilot.
action_items: Lena Park: Share SOC2 + network diagram + security pack by 2026-11-12
Marco Alvarez: Draft pilot test plan and sample load script by 2026-11-13
Evan Cole: Provide representative p95/p99 latency targets and peak qps by 2026-11-12
Marta Ruiz: Confirm KMS/HSM vendor constraints by 2026-11-15
next_steps: Redwood to send security and architecture docs
Schedule a 2-hour bench test next week for hosted and private variants
Agree pilot SLOs and traffic patterns
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-11-10 16:00 UTC | Duration: 52 mins | Attendees: Lena, Marco (Redwood); Priya, Evan, Marta, Luis (Quantum Ledger)

00:00 Lena: Hey everyone thanks for joining, um we're excited to chat through reliability constraints and where Redwood might fit. quick round of intros please.
00:09 Priya: Hi, i'm priya, head of platform at Quantum Ledger. we run most inference services for our contract reconciliation product.
00:15 Evan: Evan cole, SRE. we own the infra and SLOs.
00:19 Marta: Marta, CISO. i'll focus on encryption, KMS, audit logs.
00:24 Luis: Luis, eng lead on the model serving team.
00:27 Lena: Great. Marco, do you want to kick off with a short overview of our modes?
00:31 Marco: Sure. Redwood provides hosted API, dedicated reserved pools, and private deployment in customer VPCs or on-prem. For reliability specifically, we have smart routing, model variants for fallbacks, and built-in circuit breakers and prefix / KV caching to reduce tail latencies.
00:48 Priya: Quick question — when you say private deployment in VPC, is the control plane still in Redwood? data plane? like what lives where?
00:57 Marco: Good q. Optionally the control plane can be mediate— sorry — the control plane remains with Redwood for orchestrations, but the data plane, including model servers and KV cache, runs in your VPC. You can also opt for an air-gapped package where both are customer-managed. Some customers run the private agent that reports minimal telemetry back.
01:18 Marta: So that means telemetry and logs are configurable and we can keep PII traces out? we need audit logs and narrow retention.
01:26 Marco: Yes, per-route audit logs and retention policies are configurable. We integrate with customer KMS for key use and can disable trace payloads.
01:35 Luis: Operationally, our big worry is a zone outage in eu-west-1. We need graceful degradation and failover to another region without losing SLAs for our paying customers. what's your multi-region play?
01:47 Marco: We support region-based routing with active-active or active-passive. For active-active we recommend sticky routing with dual writes for cache warming; for active-passive we do automated health checks and failover with traffic steering. There's a tradeoff: active-active requires cross-region data sync for KV cache which increases complexity.
02:08 Evan: When you failover, what happens to in-flight requests and KV cache warmup? i've seen 10s of seconds of p99 spikes during switchover with other vendors.
02:18 Marco: Good point. We have a failover path that tries warm-start via cached prefixes — we checkpoint KV cache and use prefix priming to reduce cold-window. still small p99 spikes can happen depending on sequence lengths. We also support model-variant fallback where we fall back to a smaller quantized variant to preserve latency but with slightly different quality.
02:41 Priya: Smaller model fallback is acceptable for internal users but our external SLA customers expect fidelity. So we need a policy matrix: if region down for <5m do X, >5m do Y. can you codify that?
02:52 Marco: Yes, rollout policies are policy-driven. You can set route-level fallbacks: e.g. 0-30s retry local, 30-300s redirect to secondary region with smaller model, >300s return cached answer or degrade service gracefully. We have telemetry hooks so you can observe quality regressions.
03:12 Lena: On SLAs — what do folks expect? Evan — what are your p95/p99 targets?
03:16 Evan: For critical endpoints p95 < 120ms, p99 < 350ms under steady state at peak qps (we're talking 200 qps burst). And we want <1% error budget monthly.
03:29 Marco: Hosted will typically meet latency for small models; for p99 at high QPS you'll want dedicated or private with tuned batching. Dedicated gives predictable throughput and you can reserve warm pool capacity.
03:43 Priya: Can dedicated live in our cloud account or is that still in Redwood tenancy?
03:49 Marco: Dedicated is a reserved pool in Redwood's infrastructure but you get capacity isolation. For absolute control, private deploy in your VPC is the way. Many enterprise customers start on dedicated and then shift to private once the SLA and compliance boxes are ticked.
04:02 Marta: About compliance — SOC2, ISO? and do you support customer-managed keys (HSM)?
04:08 Lena: We are SOC2 Type II. We have ISO in progress. We support KMS integrations and offer an HSM-backed option in private deployments. We'll send the security pack after the call.
04:19 Marta: Also need SAML SSO and RBAC scoping for who can roll model versions.
04:24 Marco: RBAC and SSO are supported; you can restrict rollouts by role and set canary percentages tied to user groups.
04:31 Luis: One technical ask — can Redwood's routing decide at inference time to route to a different model based on sequence length or estimated latency?
04:39 Marco: Yes, policy routing can inspect metadata like sequence length, tenant tier, or estimated cost and route accordingly. So you can route long sequences to a high-memory cluster or route premium customers to lower-latency pools.
04:52 Priya: For our pilot we want to evaluate hosted vs private with the same model weights. Is that straightforward?
04:58 Marco: You can pin model versions and we can replicate the model to a private agent. The runtime behavior should be equivalent except for network egress differences. We'll coordinate binary/quantization versions.
05:10 Evan: Network egress — if a private agent sits in our VPC, do you require NAT or some special endpoints for pull/push?
05:18 Marco: The agent fetches model bits from your storage or from a signed Redwood bucket depending on config. For metrics/health, the agent can push to an internal telemetry endpoint or to Redwood's control plane via an outbound secure channel. We can also support VPC endpoints to avoid public egress.
05:35 Priya: Let's talk failure modes — say a model process OOMs on a node, or a whole rack fails. how do you route?
05:42 Marco: Runtime supervising detects OOMs and retries on another replica; if it's systemic we trigger circuit breakers at the route-level. The circuit breaker can shift traffic to a fallback model variant or to a cached response. You can also configure automatic gradual traffic ramp-down to avoid cascading failures.
06:00 Evan: Do you have built-in chaos testing or sim hooks? we run chaos on our side but would be good to coordinate.
06:06 Marco: We have a chaos sim playbook for customers; not fully automated but we can run scenario tests during pilots. We'll share sample scenarios.
06:14 Priya: On metrics, what do we get? token-level latency, per-route p99, cost per token?
06:20 Marco: Yes, token-level and request-level latencies, cost breakdowns, per-model dashboards, traces, and error analysis. You can export to prometheus or datadog.
06:29 Luis: About rollout windows — if we do a rollout and quality regresses, can we rollback automatically?
06:34 Marco: Yes, automatic rollback triggers on defined quality regressions. You can set a canary threshold by quality metrics or latency.
06:41 Marta: Storage of prompts and responses — we need prompt redaction and option to disable storing payloads in the control plane. Is that available?
06:50 Marco: Yes, private deploys can avoid storing payloads centrally; hosted can redact or not persist. We'll include the payload retention options in the security doc.
06:59 Priya: Cost considerations — will private be significantly more expensive?
07:04 Marco: Private has higher fixed costs (infra and egress) but gives predictable p99 and isolation. Dedicated sits in the middle: lower cost than private but less control. We can model unit economics for your workload once we have a representative prompt profile.
07:20 Evan: For the pilot, can you simulate our peak spikes? we see bursts that double baseline in minutes.
07:26 Marco: Yes, pilot load scripts can reproduce spike patterns. We'll ask for historical request traces or a synthetic pattern.
07:33 Priya: We need SLA language — uptime, latency SLOs, and credits. do you provide SLA templates?
07:39 Lena: We have SLA templates for Dedicated and Private. Hosted has standard SLA but it's generally lower SLO guarantees. We'll share contract language.
07:46 Marta: I'm concerned about cross-region data replication for cache — from a compliance perspective we want to avoid copying certain PII.
07:55 Marco: You can restrict which routes replicate cache and which don't. For sensitive routes, prefer active-passive with cache disabled for cross-region. We can also deploy per-region private agents so data never leaves the region.
08:12 Luis: What's the warm pool behavior? if we spin down for cost savings, how long to warm back up?
08:18 Marco: Warm pool can be configured; with pre-warmed reserved capacity you get almost instant readiness. If you fully scale to zero, it depends on model size — a large LLM could take tens of seconds to a few minutes to warm.
08:32 Evan: Do you support model quantization at runtime? switches between float16 and int8?
08:37 Marco: Yes, we support quantized variants. For fallback we often route to an int8 variant for lower latency. Quality differences are model-dependent.
08:45 Priya: For our pilot success criteria we want: p95/p99 within agreed thresholds, less than 2x cost increase for fallback behavior, and no cross-region PII replication. Can you accept these as pilot SLOs?
08:57 Lena: Sounds reasonable. We'll formalize and include thresholds.
09:02 Priya: Another operational ask — who gets paged in Redwood for incidents? can we map oncall and escalation?
09:08 Marco: Yes, we can integrate with pagerduty and define escalation paths. For private agents you also own some oncall depending on deployment mode.
09:16 Evan: One more — do you have a mechanism to throttle tenants to preserve p99 for high-priority customers?
09:21 Marco: Tenant-level throttling and rate limits exist; you can set per-tenant quotas and divert lower-tier tenants to cheaper model variants automatically.
09:29 Priya: Ok let's get tactical — we'll run two pilots: hosted at first to validate traffic shaping, then private agent in our eu-west-1 with KMS and no cross-region replication. timeline two weeks each?
09:40 Lena: Timeline seems doable. Marco will own the pilot plan.
09:44 Marco: I'll draft the test plan and sample load script. I'll include scenarios: zone failover, node OOM, cache coldstart, and model variant fallback.
09:56 Marta: I'll review security pack and come back with any gating items.
09:59 Priya: Any objections or competitors we need to call out? we evaluated MajorCloudAI but latency was inconsistent.
10:06 Lena: Noted. we'll include benchmark comparisons where relevant.
10:10 Evan: Ok wrapping — can you also include instrumentation for quality checks? we need a diffs dashboard versus golden responses.
10:16 Marco: Yes, quality regression alerts tied to prompt sets. we'll include how we compute delta.
10:22 Lena: Great. recap of next steps: security docs, pilot plan, schedule bench test, agree SLOs.
10:28 Priya: Thanks everyone. we'll aim to get you our traffic traces and latency targets by Thursday.
10:33 Lena: Thanks — we'll follow up with calendar and docs.
10:36 Meeting end.

Notes: transcription included some speaker attribution guesses; timings are approximate. There are a few mis-heard words (e.g., 'mediate' for 'maintain') but content is intact.
